stops.name: Jerusalem, the walls thrown down by his own brother
stops.campa: Fearing that a crusader army flush with Damietta might now strike at Jerusalem itself and hold it against every Ayyubid counter-siege, al-Mu'azzam Isa orders the walls of the Holy City thrown down with his own garrison's hands, the Dome of the Rock left standing amid rubble, the Franks denied a fortress even if they take the ground. Al-Kamil, still repeating his offer of the city to the enemy camp, watches his brother unmake by demolition what he is trying to give away by treaty — the two Ayyubid strategies, cession and destruction, arriving at the same conclusion: that Jerusalem, undefended, is worth less as a possession than as a gift withheld.

stops.name: Al-Mansurah, the sultan regroups, the offer renewed
stops.campa: At al-Mansurah, a new town he raises on the Nile above Damietta expressly to bar the road to Cairo, al-Kamil rebuilds his army through a slow year of standoff. Embassies pass back and forth across the lines; the sultan repeats his terms — Jerusalem, the True Cross, a lasting truce — to a crusader camp that is itself split, its soldiers and many of its knights eager to accept, its legate Pelagius and the arriving Italians still holding out for the full conquest of Egypt that a promised army under the Emperor Frederick has not yet sent. Al-Kamil waits, fortifies, and does not attack; he has learned that Egypt's flood is a weapon he need only leave loaded.

stops.name: Al-Mansurah, the crusaders march on Cairo
stops.campa: Against al-Kamil's terms and against the counsel of his own field commander John of Brienne, Pelagius orders the army south from Damietta toward Cairo itself, certain that one more push completes the conquest Damietta began. Al-Kamil falls back before them without a major battle, ceding ground he has no intention of holding, watching the crusader host advance deeper into the Delta between the branching arms of the Nile — into the exact country, flat and canal-cut and floodable, that he and his engineers have spent two years quietly preparing.

stops.name: The Nile dams opened, the trap closes
stops.campa: With the crusader army strung out on the narrow ground between the Nile and the Bahr al-Saghir canal, al-Kamil gives the order his engineers have waited two years to carry out: the dams and sluices upstream are opened, and the annual Nile flood, already swollen, pours into the canals around the Frankish camp. Within days the ground the crusaders stand on has become an island, their supply lines to Damietta cut, their siege engines and horses mired, retreat itself impossible without ships he has already moved to block the river. No battle is fought; the river alone does what two years of siegecraft could not.

stops.name: Al-Mansurah, the crusader surrender
stops.campa: Starving, flooded, and surrounded, Pelagius and John of Brienne sue for terms they refused two years running. Al-Kamil, holding every advantage, does not humiliate them: he offers the same bargain in reverse — an eight-year truce, the return of Damietta and every prisoner, in exchange for the crusader army's unmolested evacuation of Egypt. He feeds the starving Franks from his own stores before they march out. Oliver of Paderborn, who watched Christian soldiers die of hunger within sight of the sultan's provisions, will write plainly of the mercy shown a beaten enemy.
stops.quote: Who could doubt that such goodness, friendship and charity come from God? Men whose parents, sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, had died in agony at our hands, whose lands we took, whom we drove naked from their homes, revived us with their own food when we were dying of hunger and showered us with kindness even when we were in their power.
stops.quote_source: Oliver of Paderborn, Historia Damiatina, on al-Kamil's provisioning of the surrendered army

stops.name: Damietta restored, the truce of eight years
stops.campa: The crusader army marches out of Egypt and Damietta is handed back on the eighth of September, exactly the terms al-Kamil offered before the city ever fell in the first place, now bought back at the cost of a war that gained the Franks nothing they did not already have. He rides into the recovered port at the head of his own household, the True Cross among the returned relics, the Fifth Crusade ended not by a decisive battle but by a river he chose the hour to release. Egypt is his again, whole; the offer he made and was refused three times has cost his enemies everything and himself almost nothing.

stops.name: Cairo, trade with Venice and the works of peace
stops.campa: With the Franks gone from Egyptian soil, al-Kamil turns to the labor he prefers to war: he renews and extends trade agreements with Venice and the other Italian maritime cities, opening Alexandria and Damietta again to the merchants whose galleys had lately carried an invading army. Customs revenue rebuilds a treasury drained by three years of siege; canals and dikes broken in the flood he himself unleashed are repaired; the same engineering that trapped an army now waters the fields that feed it. He governs, his own court remembers, as a man more interested in the welfare of the ruled than in the glory of the ruler.

stops.name: Damascus, the rift with al-Mu'azzam over strategy
stops.campa: The brother who saved his throne before Damietta becomes, in peace, his rival: al-Mu'azzam of Damascus resents al-Kamil's willingness to trade land for treaties and courts the sultan's enemies in turn, even flirting with alliance against Egypt's dealings with the Franks and, more dangerously, with the Khwarazmian adventurer Jalal al-Din to the east. The house of Ayyub, never more than a confederation of cousins under a single eldest claim, strains again along its oldest fault line — the same rivalry between Cairo and Damascus that split Saladin's own sons a generation before. Al-Kamil, watching, begins to draw his youngest brother al-Ashraf of the Jazira toward Egypt's side of the quarrel.

stops.name: Damascus, the death of al-Mu'azzam opens the door
stops.campa: Al-Mu'azzam dies in Damascus, leaving Syria and Palestine to his young son al-Nasir Dawud, a nephew with neither his father's army nor his standing among the family's elders. The rivalry that shadowed al-Kamil's decade of peace is broken at a stroke; he and al-Ashraf, closing ranks against the inexperienced heir, begin to plan the recovery of Damascus for the elder branch of the house. It is this quarrel over the nephew's inheritance, more than any crusader army, that will decide the fate of Jerusalem in the two years to come — a city about to be handed twice over as small change in a family settlement.

stops.name: Cairo, Fakhr al-Din sent to Sicily
stops.campa: Needing a counterweight against his brother al-Mu'azzam while the Damascus quarrel still burns, al-Kamil opens correspondence with an unlikely partner: Frederick II Hohenstaufen, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Sicily, sends embassies proposing an alliance, and al-Kamil answers in kind, dispatching his trusted emir Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh to the Sicilian court to treat directly with a Christian ruler raised among Arabic tutors and known already for his taste in Muslim learning. The sultan is playing a game two moves deep: a German army arriving as his ally against Damascus is worth infinitely more to him than the same army arriving as an enemy at Damietta again.

stops.name: Cairo, the emperor's questions on the heavens
stops.campa: Between the clauses of alliance, Frederick sends al-Kamil something no crusader king has sent before: questions of philosophy and natural science, on the eternity of the world, the nature of the soul, the working of the heavens, put to the sultan's scholars as one court of learning to another. Al-Kamil, who founded a madrasa for the study of tradition and loves nothing better than an evening's disputation, answers with evident pleasure, setting his own philosophers and astronomers to the emperor's puzzles. It is, on both sides, a genuine exchange of minds conducted in the pauses of a war neither man especially wants to finish fighting.

stops.name: Cairo, the gift of the sphere of stars
stops.campa: Among the gifts that pass between the two courts through Fakhr al-Din's hands, one becomes legend on both sides of the sea: a tent pierced through with small holes, so that a lamp lit within casts the pattern of the stars and planets across its own dark ceiling, a portable heaven a prince can carry to camp. Al-Kamil, whose interest in astronomy is no courtly affectation, sends it as a token between minds that understand each other better across the space of an ocean and a faith than either does with half his own barons — a fitting emblem of a friendship built entirely on parchment and never once on a shared table.
